title: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña waves after a meeting with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas, on September 19, 2026.
                
                    Federico Parra/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Federico Parra/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money.   Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers — more than half of the country's adult population.    He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country, but legislators said he jeopardized state assets and benefitted himself through his connection to the bank.    
   Ueno Bank previously said more than a million people opened bank accounts for the first time using its services, which included generous cash back offers on groceries.   
   A trial has proceeded against Peña, and he appeared before prosecutors Saturday morning. The last president ousted from office was Fernando Lugo in 2012.    Peña has denied any wrongdoing but on Thursday he announced his resignation. Lawmakers refused to accept that resignation, and instead moved forward with the country's impeachment process.   At proceedings inside the country's Senate Friday, legislators unanimously found Peña guilty of malfeasance in office, according to the Senate's website.   Prosecutors then accused him of a breach of trust, among other charges, before placing him under house arrest.   "I want to apologize to the Paraguayan people if I have failed you," Peña said in a speech posted to social media.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Demonstrators burn an image depicting Paraguay's President Santiago Pena, during a protest over the banking crisis and his resignation, at the main square in the surroundings of the National Congress in Asuncion, on November 5, 2026.
                
                    Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, was sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028. In a speech on Friday, he announced he would take action to compensate people whose money was lost in the bank's collapse.   Paraguay's central bank said it seized control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday because its solvency ratio, an assessment of a company's long-term financial viability, no longer met legal standards.   
   Protests erupted across Asunción, the country's capital city, following the seizure.   NPR's John Otis and Catherine Osborn contributed reporting to this story.

title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
description: FILE - President Donald Trump waves alon
body:
FILE - President Donald Trump waves alongside Dana White, president and CEO of UFC, as they arrive for the UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House, June 14, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Mark Schiefelbein/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Schiefelbein/AP
    

   
   WEST PALM BEACH, Fla.  — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.   Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.   
   White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.   When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."   He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."   Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."   The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.   Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"   
   While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.   Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.   Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.   The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.   The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.   Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.   He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.   
   "It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.   White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

title: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats
description: James Talarico speaks on election night
body:
James Talarico speaks on election night in Austin, Texas. Talarico won his race for U.S. Senate by 12 percentage points overall, but when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.   It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.   But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.   
   How young voters powered Democrats to victory    Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.   However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference, is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.   The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points, however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.   
   Explaining the massive shift from 2024   When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.   But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.   
   Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18-29 year olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.   The young voters Trump lost    Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.   
   Democrats made gains with some young voters that backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.     Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.   How the election results broke down by age     Loading... 
   The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.   "The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."   Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.   
   "I also think we shouldn't over read what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."   By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.   "Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.   
   "They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

schema.headline: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats

title: President of The Heritage Foundation looks ahead to the future of the GOP
description: Kevin Roberts, the president of the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation, talks about the organization's priorities and hopes for th
body:
Kevin Roberts, the president of the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation, talks about the organization's priorities and hopes for the future of the Republican Party and its policies.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:  After the midterms this week, Republicans are asking, where do we go from here? The conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation has long provided answers to that question ever since it wrote the mandate for leadership for President Reagan in 1981. The foundation has informed many of the Trump administration's priorities through the policy blueprint known as Project 2025.Kevin Roberts is a political strategist and was a key architect of Project 2025. He's led The Heritage Foundation as its president since 2021. He joins us now to talk about the path forward for Republicans. Welcome.KEVIN ROBERTS: Thanks, Rob, for having me. It's a pleasure.SCHMITZ: So before we get to the midterm results, we had news yesterday. Susie Wiles is out as President Trump's chief of staff. Stephen Miller is in. What does this tell us about the path forward for the Trump administration?ROBERTS: Well, it's a great promotion of a great patriot, Stephen Miller, because what it signals to not just the radical-left majority coming into Congress, but for all of us on the political right, is that President Trump and his administration are not rolling over. I know that people who are on the political left disagree maybe with Stephen Miller with everything. They probably disagree with me and Heritage with everything. He's an extremely competent, politically conservative, very intellectual policymaker, and for those of us on the political right who are charting the way forward after this week's major defeat, I think Stephen's a perfect choice.SCHMITZ: Why the change?ROBERTS: I think what the president is signaling is that it is a new era, and he needs Stephen's acumen, particularly his ability to be on offense even with a large Democrat majority in the House and Senate.SCHMITZ: So I think it's safe to say here that the midterms did not go the way that the president hoped. How do these results shape the plans that you and The Heritage Foundation are making for Republicans going forward?ROBERTS: Yeah, even for people who were more pessimistic than I am, I actually thought the midterms would be OK. Obviously, I was wrong about that. But the people who were more pessimistic did not think that it would be a defeat on the scale. And so the first thing that we have to do is just to read reality truthfully. You acknowledge that, at least in terms of messaging, the message from the political right, from the administration, was insufficient.I happen to think that the Iran war was a major problem even though I'm supportive of the Iran war, I've been saying since April and May that the administration needs to find a way to declare victory because the economic consequences that have aggravated existing inflationary concerns that Trump inherited were a real problem.And so moving forward, what the administration needs to do is not just handle some of the lawfare and what I'm sure will be some nonsense coming from the Democrat majorities, but articulate a policy vision that gets back to that domestic policy, especially kitchen-table economics issues.SCHMITZ: So on election night - you know, talking about Iran here - you told my colleague Mary Louise Kelly that larger-scale Republican defeats are not a wholesale rejection of President Trump's agenda but instead a, quote, "complaint by voters about the economic consequences of the Iran conflict." You just mentioned that. What needs to change when it comes to the U.S. war in Iran?ROBERTS: Well, I've been saying since May or June, along with my colleagues - national security colleagues at Heritage, that No. 1, we're supportive of the war. No. 2, the president could have declared victory given the military achievements as early as May or June. And had he done that, I think we would have been able to see the diminished economic disadvantages that have come from the war in time to affect - in a positive way, from our vantage point - the election. It's really important that the president and the administration make that declaration soon because it will take, according to my economist colleagues at Heritage, several months for the inflationary pressure brought on by energy prices, energy inflation to come down.I think that what you do - to cut to the chase here, Rob - is you obviously leave some naval and air superiority in Iran, maybe not to the extent of the deployment now. And when the Iranians misbehave, you can zing them with cruise missile attacks, and you also pair that with what has been a really good economic strangulation campaign by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.SCHMITZ: The election's been largely understood as a referendum on the economy and the cost of living for average Americans. Gas prices - because of the war with Iran and also because of President Trump's tariffs, which you were initially against before you embraced them - have been a problem. Would you embrace a pivot away from tariffs at this point?ROBERTS: No, I'm very supportive. We at Heritage are very supportive of a true reciprocal tariff regime. And, you know, if we were building the tariff policy - and we said this going back to the so-called Liberation Day - that we would focus on the 5 to 10 worst transgressors of, quote-unquote, "free trade." And had the administration focused on that, I think the American people, maybe even a bipartisan way, would have really embraced that. I think there's still a future for that policy, but it's going to have to be, you know, more circumscribed than it's been.SCHMITZ: You know, when we're talking about the economy and the problems of the economy right now, you have sort of boiled it down to Iran. Are there any other problems in the economy that you see?ROBERTS: Oh, yeah. The point about Iran - so thanks for the opportunity to follow up on that - is not that it, in and of itself, has caused all of our economic difficulties or worries. It's that it's aggravated some long-standing existing problems. It's just objectively true, to put respective politics off to the side, that the Trump administration inherited very high inflation from the previous administration, and all of those economic measures were improving the week before the war in Iran. In fact, our chief economist at Heritage, Dr. E.J. Antoni, has predicted that there would have been a Trump economic boom had he not started the war in Iran. The point is that Iran, especially by increasing energy prices, aggravated those inflationary pressures.SCHMITZ: You know, another question I have for you has to do with corruption. You know, corruption was also at the top of voters' concerns going into these midterm I was in Hungary earlier this year, where corruption also played a big part in Viktor Orbán's routing there. People see the president and his family benefiting from cryptocurrency, other investments. You know, what is your reaction to how this has damaged Republicans at the polls?ROBERTS: Well, just looking at the exit polls, it's - American voters are saying, obviously, this is a concern, and you draw a very accurate parallel, Rob, with Hungary. I think, as you know, the Orbán government's policies were very good, but, you know, they had been in power for 16 years, and there clearly was corruption that was a problem.And so it's really important moving forward - not just for the administration, not just for Republican allies in Congress, but also for the incoming Democrat majority in the House and Senate - to remember that this has been a very anti-power election. The American people are saying, we're tired of this. It isn't just a problem on the right. It isn't just a problem on the left. Thank goodness, Americans are paying attention, and they want leaders who are not engaged.SCHMITZ: The agenda for the right used to be really clear - you know, smaller government, lower taxes, free trade. Project 2025 was a huge effort to define this new post-Reagan conservative movement. But you've had challenges, I think, keeping everyone aligned. It seems there's, like, sort of a generational civil war happening in the party with influencers and other right-wing think tanks all trying to define the party. Looking ahead to 2028, what is Heritage's core vision? How do you see regaining voter trust here?ROBERTS: Yeah, you're definitely right about tensions on the right. And to state the obvious, President Trump will be leaving the stage in early 2029, and so all of us who are conservative policy leaders are trying to articulate a vision for the future. For us at Heritage, Rob, we want to do two things. No. 1, we want to focus on those economic matters. We want to actually provide the policy solutions for Americans' legitimate worries about affordability.And secondly, we are gratified that still a slight majority of Americans think that socialist policies are bad. But we're worried that somewhere between 40- and 45% of Americans are willing to try those policies. We have to go explain why those policies of socialists - legitimate socialists - are problematic rather than just, as has been customary of conservative elected officials this cycle, pointing to socialists, pointing to neo-Marxists and just labeling them as that. The American people actually want answers.And so that's a way of saying, to give you the bottom line here, that at Heritage, we're trying to keep things simple. We're trying to address the kitchen-table issues. We will continue to preach for a more restrained national security posture, which, until the Iran War, this Trump administration has done a very good job of.SCHMITZ: So are you going to put a stake in the ground here and say whether you'll support Marco Rubio or JD Vance for 2028?ROBERTS: (Laughter) Nice try, but that's not something we do or can do at Heritage. We don't get into endorsements. What we can say is, if - whoever the conservative standard bearer is in 2028, whoever the conservative officials are running for office in 2028, we want them to be talking about these issues that address these affordability and economic concerns.SCHMITZ: That is Kevin Roberts, president of the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation. Thank you.ROBERTS: Thank you.

title: Texas's 'Blue Tsunami' has former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke 'over the moon'
description: NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke about how past efforts by him and other Democrats helped the party win big
body:
NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke about how past efforts by him and other Democrats helped the party win big in Texas in the midterms.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:  While Texas' populist roots may have laid the foundation for Democratic victories in the state, they weren't the only factor that helped Texas Democrats win on Tuesday. Former Texas congressman and presidential candidate Beto O'Rourke has helped pave the way for Democrat victories in the Lone Star State. You might remember his 2018 bid to unseat longstanding Republican Senator Ted Cruz. Ultimately, he lost by just a few percentage points. In 2022, he ran against Governor Greg Abbott and again lost, that time by only a slightly larger margin. Beto O'Rourke joins us now. Welcome.BETO O'ROURKE: It's good to be with you.SCHMITZ: So I feel like you have been out of the national spotlight for a while, but perhaps that's because you've been hard at work on the ground there in Texas mobilizing voters. Tell us about that.O'ROURKE: After the Senate race, we asked ourselves, what would it take to win in Texas? And from that, we started a group called Powered By People, and it's thousands of folks - many of whom volunteered on that Senate race - who get trained as volunteer deputy registrars, meet young people in person, get them registered and then, importantly, stay in touch with them and help them overcome the obstacles in a state that makes it harder than any other in the nation for young people to register and to vote, to help them participate in our politics.SCHMITZ: Young folks showed up big time for Democrats this cycle. An NBC exit poll shows that 79% of voters under the age of 30 voted for Talarico. What do you think appealed to that demographic?O'ROURKE: I think, first and foremost, James Talarico, who described this contest as not between a Democrat and a Republican or right versus left, but top versus bottom. When I spend time on these college campuses or at (inaudible) or clubs with young people as we help them to get registered and I ask them what's important to them, they are absolutely disgusted with the concentration of wealth and privilege and power in this country. They ask me about the Epstein files and say, you know, how can the wealthiest, most powerful men rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity? How is it that we're at war again in the Middle East? Why are we complicit in this genocide in Gaza? Why is no one doing anything about these things?And then at home in Texas, the minimum wage is 7.25. It's the hardest state in the nation in which to see a doctor, and schoolteachers are working two or three jobs to make ends meet. These aren't Republican or Democrat issues. They're issues of basic justice, and I think that young people have the most acute sense of what is right or wrong. They are impatient with excuses or equivocation or blaming it on one party or another. They want solutions, and they want people to deliver.SCHMITZ: That's interesting. I mean, this is something that we spoke with our previous guest, David Griscom - he's an author in Texas - about, that economic populism was one of the reasons that James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won both the Senate and gubernatorial election. Is there anything that Democrats can learn from how this played out and what really matters to Texans?O'ROURKE: I think the takeaway is it is incredibly important for Democrats now in power to deliver for the people they represent in ways that they can feel immediately. So raising the minimum wage - if you're working for $7.25 an hour, you're probably working two or three of those jobs to make ends meet. Raising that minimum wage will be felt immediately.You know, if you can't afford to see a doctor right now, and you're suffering as a result of that, being able to, through Medicaid expansion, see a provider - that's going to change your life immediately. And the follow-on effects of being able to afford tuition or down payment on a home or an automobile, these are significant material differences in people's lives.And so we have high expectations for Gina and James. And really, as you probably know, every single statewide office was won by a Democrat. The Democrats also picked a majority in the state House. They now have the opportunity to deliver for people. And so while we're excited and we're celebrating their victories, we're also understanding there's accountability, responsibility, and the clock is ticking.SCHMITZ: You obviously had a lot to do with this popularity of Democrats that we are seeing right now. I mean, you, of course, ran for Senate. You ran for governor. You lost time and time again for both of those races. But a lot in the background was gained. How is this feeling for you right now, seeing these wins?O'ROURKE: I'm over the moon. I mean, you know, my wife, Amy, and I, in 2016, when Trump won - I happened to be in Congress at the time - we looked at each other and we said, we have got to do something more. What we've been doing so far serving in Congress is insufficient to the task at hand, this threat of authoritarianism and fascism and the rise of this oligarchy in America. We needed to do something.And from that was born this crazy snowball's-chance-in-Texas idea of running for Senate in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1988. And I was joined by hundreds of thousands - and by the end, millions - of my fellow Texans who believed in that dream. And so it wasn't so much, you know, should Beto O'Rourke serve in the Senate or, you know, my name on an office or on the ballot. It is, can we change this state? And by extension, given the outsized importance of Texas, can we change this country?SCHMITZ: Well, Beto O'Rourke, since I've got you here, I should ask you whether you have plans to run for president in 2028.O'ROURKE: No, I don't, but I am going to be involved one way or another. This extraordinary experiment 250 years in the making that is the product of so much service and sacrifice and struggle - all of us must do all that we can to keep it going. So that's my mission. That's what I'm going to be focused on. And wherever I can be useful or helpful, that's where you'll find me.SCHMITZ: That is former Texas Congressman Beto O'Rourke. Thanks so much for joining us.O'ROURKE: Thank you.
